syntaxCards.note: Min-heap pops the smallest element. Java and C++ compare with greater<int>() and greater<>(). Python heapq is always a min-heap; use negative values for a max-heap.

snippets.python:
import heapq
heapq.heappush(pq, v)   # min-heap
heapq.heappop(pq)    # smallest
# max-heap: push -v, pop, negate

syntaxCards.note: Two pointers need a monotone invariant: if the sum is too small, left must move right; if too large, right must move left. Sorting first is what makes the monotone step valid.
Prefer the lower-bound half-open form. It has no off-by-one branch and returns the first index where the predicate holds.
BFS with a Queue visits in wave order, so the first time you reach a node is its shortest distance. DFS with recursion or a Stack is for reachability and cycle structure, not distance.
Variable-width windows: add the entering element, then shrink while the window is invalid. The shrink condition must reference the same predicate you tested to expand.
When you need to know whether a value was seen before, a HashMap costs O(1) average instead of a Set scan. Reserve capacity when the input size is known to avoid rehashing.
Write the state definition as a sentence before any code. Tabulation fills a table bottom-up; memoisation recurses top-down. Both compute the same states.
A stack gives O(1) push and pop and surfaces the most recent unmatched opener. Use an ArrayDeque in Java rather than a legacy Stack so insertion order is well defined.

snippets.python:
st = []
st.append(c)
o = st.pop()
empty = not st

syntaxCards.note: The choose-recurse-undo cycle is the whole algorithm. Push before recursing and always pop after, in the reverse order of the push, or sibling branches inherit corrupted state.

Recursion mirrors the tree shape. Preorder visits node then children, inorder is required for sorted binary trees, postorder computes values that depend on both subtrees. Depth can exceed the stack limit on skewed trees, so an explicit stack is safer in interviews.

snippets.python:
def preorder(node, out):
    if node is None: return
    out.append(node.val)
    preorder(node.left, out)
    preorder(node.right, out)

syntaxCards.note: x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, which yields a running count of set bits. For a power of two, x & (x - 1) is zero.

snippets.python:
x = n
count = 0
while x:
    x &= x - 1
    count += 1
is_pow2 = n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

syntaxCards.note: For merge problems sort by start time. For sweep problems such as meeting rooms, sort by start and compare each start against a max-heap of end times.
A greedy choice must be locally safe, so it needs a proof: usually an exchange argument showing the greedy pick can be substituted into an optimal solution without loss.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Each input has exactly one solution and you may not use the same element twice.
problems.keyIdea: Trade a nested scan for a remembered past. Store each value with its index as you go, so the complement of the current value is a single lookup rather than a full search.

ladder.label: Brute force
ladder.why: Check every pair. Correct and obvious, but you scan the rest of the array once per element.

ladder.label: Sorted two pointers
ladder.why: Sorting makes the sum monotone in each cursor, so one pointer can be discarded per step. Sorting dominates the cost.

code.python:
s = sorted(nums)
l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
while l < r:
    if s[l] + s[r] == target: return [l, r]
    if s[l] + s[r] < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1

ladder.label: Hash map single pass
ladder.why: One pass, no sorting. You pay O(n) space to buy back the O(n log n) sort and the second scan.

hints: You need the complement of the current value. What structure makes finding it O(1)?
As you scan left to right, store each value together with its index.
Before storing nums[i], check whether target - nums[i] is already stored. That ordering is what prevents reusing one element.
A HashMap of value to index. One pass over the array.
Pseudocode: for each i, look up need in seen; if found return [seen[need], i]; else seen[nums[i]] = i.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
problems.keyIdea: The window must stay duplicate-free. When a repeat appears, advance the left edge past the previous occurrence rather than restarting the scan.

ladder.label: Check every substring
ladder.why: Enumerate all O(n^2) substrings and verify each with an O(n) set. Quadratic start times linear work.

ladder.label: Sliding window with a set
ladder.why: The outer scan is now linear, but shrinking one character at a time and re-checking the whole window stays quadratic.

code.python:
best = 0; l = 0; seen = set()
for r, ch in enumerate(s):
    while ch in seen:
        seen.remove(s[l]); l += 1
    seen.add(ch)
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)
return best

ladder.label: Sliding window with last-seen map
ladder.why: Remember where each character last appeared. The left edge jumps straight to one past that index instead of creeping forward one character at a time.

hints: What invariant must hold for the current window?
The window can never contain a duplicate. When adding a character that already exists inside it, the left edge must move.
Do not shrink one character at a time. Jump the left edge directly past the previous occurrence of the repeating character.
A map from character to its last seen index. On a repeat, set left to lastSeen[c] + 1.
Pseudocode: for each r, if last[s[r]] >= l then l = last[s[r]] + 1; last[s[r]] = r; best = max(best, r - l + 1).

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement: Given a string containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. An input string is valid if open brackets are closed by the same type of bracket and in the correct order.
problems.keyIdea: Nesting is strictly last-in-first-out, which is exactly what a stack guarantees. Push openers, and every closer must match the most recent unmatched opener.

ladder.label: Rescan on every mismatch
ladder.why: On finding a mismatch, restart validation from the beginning. Correct but re-checks the same prefix repeatedly.

ladder.label: Counting brackets
ladder.why: Counts total openings against closings. It detects a missing or extra bracket but silently accepts '{]}' because the ordering is never checked.

code.python:
opening = sum(s.count(c) for c in '({[')
closing = sum(s.count(c) for c in ')}]')
return opening == closing

ladder.label: Stack with type matching
ladder.why: Push every opener, then require each closer to match the stack top. Ordering becomes structurally enforced rather than counted.

hints: Which data structure matches strict nesting order exactly?
Openers must close in reverse order of opening. That is the definition of a stack.
Push openers. On a closer, the stack top must be its partner, or the string is invalid.
A stack of characters, plus a map from closer to opener.
Pseudocode: push '(' '{' '['; for any closer, if stack empty return false, else pop and compare to its partner; at the end return stack.isEmpty().

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: An array sorted in ascending order is rotated at an unknown pivot. Given the rotated array and an integer target, return the index of target if it exists, or -1 if it is not in the array. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
problems.keyIdea: At every split one half is still fully sorted. Identify which half by comparing the midpoint against the low bound, then discard the half that cannot contain the target.

ladder.label: Linear scan
ladder.why: Rotation does not affect membership testing. Ignores the sorted structure entirely and fails the stated complexity requirement.

ladder.label: Binary search then linear wrap
ladder.why: Binary search one monotonic run, then scan the tail. Correct and simple, but the scan makes worst-case behaviour unpredictable.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[m] > target: r = m - 1
    else: l = m + 1
return next((i for i, v in enumerate(nums) if v == target), -1)

ladder.label: Modified binary search
ladder.why: At least one half around the midpoint is sorted. Test that half's range against the target and discard the other, halving the window every step.

code.python:
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l <= r:
    m = (l + r) // 2
    if nums[m] == target: return m
    if nums[l] <= nums[m]:
        if nums[l] <= target < nums[m]: r = m - 1
        else: l = m + 1
    else:
        if nums[m] < target <= nums[r]: l = m + 1
        else: r = m - 1
return -1

hints: Why does ordinary binary search break on a rotated array?
Because the array is not globally sorted, the usual discard rule is no longer trustworthy. You need a different signal each step.
At any midpoint, one of the two halves is still sorted. Determine which one by comparing nums[left] to nums[mid].
If the left half is sorted, the target is either inside it or in the right half. If the right half is sorted, the opposite applies.
Pseudocode: if nums[l] <= nums[m] then range-check the left half, else range-check the right half. Narrow one bound each iteration.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations. You can return the answer in any order.
problems.keyIdea: Build the answer one position at a time. Choose an unused value for the current slot, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts from the same state.

ladder.label: Enumerate all orderings
ladder.why: Generate every arrangement directly. The factorial growth is the problem to be solved, not worked around.

ladder.label: Used-array bookkeeping
ladder.why: Same factorial cost but tracks used values explicitly, which makes the logic portable to problems with duplicate elements.

code.python:
used = [False] * len(nums)
cur = []
def bt():
    if len(cur) == len(nums):
        out.append(cur[:]); return
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if used[i]: continue
        used[i] = True; cur.append(nums[i])
        bt()
        cur.pop(); used[i] = False
bt()

ladder.label: Swap into position
ladder.why: Same asymptotics, since n! outputs must be materialised. The in-place swap removes the used array and reduces allocations per branch.

hints: What does one branch of the search tree represent?
A partial arrangement. A complete leaf is a full permutation. You need to grow the branch and then restore it.
At each level, try every value not yet used, recurse, then remove it.
The critical detail is undoing the choice. Without the undo, every sibling sees a corrupted array.
Pseudocode: if the current path is full, record it. Otherwise for each unused value: push it, recurse, pop it.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.statement: Given an m x n 2D binary grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (waters), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are surrounded by water.
problems.keyIdea: Each new unvisited land cell starts exactly one island. Flood-fill the whole connected component so it is never counted twice.

ladder.label: Repeated flood fill without marking
ladder.why: The fill explores the same component from every starting cell because nothing records that ground was already processed.

ladder.label: Flood fill with visited set
ladder.why: An explicit visited set makes the complexity provably linear, at the cost of auxiliary memory alongside the grid.

ladder.label: Iterative sink as you count
ladder.why: The sink writes its own state, so no auxiliary structure is needed. Same asymptotics as the visited set, but O(1) extra memory.

hints: How do you avoid counting one island twice?
When you find unvisited land, that cell must be the start of a brand new island. Once counted, the whole connected region is finished.
Flood fill from the starting cell, marking every land cell you touch so the outer loop skips it.
Recursive DFS is simplest but can overflow the stack on large grids. An explicit stack keeps memory on the heap.
Pseudocode: on unvisited '1', increment the count, then flood fill all connected '1' cells, marking each as '0' as you visit it.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. You can either climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
problems.keyIdea: The ways to reach step i are the ways to reach i-1 plus the ways to reach i-2, because the last move was either one or two steps. That recurrence is Fibonacci.

ladder.label: Tree of all move sequences
ladder.why: Enumerate every possible sequence of 1s and 2s. Exponential because the same subproblem recurs exponentially often.

ladder.label: Memoised recursion
ladder.why: Caching each computed value collapses the exponential recursion into a linear chain. Memoisation with recursion is the top-down form.

ladder.label: Tabulation with two variables
ladder.why: Only the previous two states are ever read, so the whole table collapses to two variables. Same linear time, constant memory.

hints: How many moves reach the final step, and who could have arrived there?
You can only arrive on step i from step i-1 with a one-step move or from step i-2 with a two-step move. Those two cases are disjoint.
Write ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) and then ask how many distinct states exist.
There are n states. A naive recursion recomputes the same states exponentially many times.
Either cache each value (top-down) or fill the values in order from step 1 (bottom-up). Note that only the last two are ever needed.
